newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian Sugar - China prices rising on Moon Festival.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar - China prices rising on Moon Festival.

text.p: The sweetest season of the year is approaching with Mid-Autumn Festival, and wholesale sugar prices in China's southern production areas are already on the rise, regional traders said on Wednesday.

In the major production area of Guangxi, in China's far southwest, ex-factory prices were quoted at 4,200 yuan ($506) a tonne compared with 4,000 yuan ($482) per tonne last week, a Chinese sugar trader said.
Mid-Autumn Festival this year falls on September 16, and is traditionally celebrated throughout China -- population 1.2 billion -- with rich, sticky, sweet moon cakes.
Traders said sugar prices usually began to rise in anticipation of the festival towards the end of August.
"But the rises started 10 days earlier this year than last year," he said, adding it remained to be seen how long the rally would last.
Sugar officials in Guangxi could not be reached for comment as they were attending an industry meeting, Reuters was told.
Traders said that most buying of bulk sugar was coming from consumption areas -- major urban centres -- where existing stocks had run low.
"They have adopted a strategy that they buy when their stocks finish and now they have very little stocks," the Chinese trader said of wholesale buyers in the consumption areas.
Consumers in Shanghai did not report any noticeable recent increases in retail sugar prices, with both granulated and more refined sugar selling at around three to four yuan per lb.
Recent bad weather in southern China, including Typhoon Victor which swept through Hong Kong at the weekend, had not affected Guangxi or Yunnan provinces, traders said.
Cane had already been planted -- harvest is November to March -- and weather had been favourable, trade sources said.
The China Sugar Association reported a 1996 crop of 6.6 million tonnes, later amended to 6.8 million.

The official China Securities newspaper reported on Tuesday that 4.96 million tonnes, or 73 percent of the crop, had already been purchased, and predicted a stable market this year, without further details.
No Chinese activity was seen on the international market, traders said.
A trader with a big Western house in Hong Kong said China had not been a big buyer of Thai raw sugar this year, and traders were now focusing on 1998, which he described as bullish.
"I think people will pay up to 100 (U.S. cents premium) for January to March (Thai raws), it is that bullish," he said.
"March-May sugar is around 90 (U.S. cents premium), but I would say the offers are still 10 points away," he said.
There was little interest in prompt delivery sugar, he said, with huge quantities of Thai raws still available.
"There's still between 200,000 and 300,000 tonnes available in Thailand on the ship so this will place some pressure on the Thai raws until after August," he said.
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai Newsroom (8621) 6279-8544
